# 2026年暑期档破百亿元 “电影+”演绎消费新活力

2026-08-18 15:02

国际商报记者 李子晨

今年暑期，上海新天地一家影院大厅人头攒动，爆米花的香气与观众的欢声笑语交织在一起。随着一场《八仙！》放映完，不少年轻观众在影院的零售区域排起长队，选购影片联名文创盲盒。在杭州上城区的一家影院，刚看完《功夫女足》的一家三口，正拿着电影票根前往商场餐厅，兑换观影专属“热血套餐”。

据灯塔专业版实时数据，截至8月16日16时59分，今年暑期档（6月1日—8月31日）总票房（含预售）突破100亿元大关，同比增长3.2%；今年暑期档观影人次达2.74亿，同比增长5.7%；平均票价36.5元，同比下降2.4%。百亿票房背后，既凸显了影视市场“以价换量”的成效，又是“电影+”新业态撬动千亿级消费大盘的生动实践。

优质供给激活多元观影需求

纵观今年暑期档，喜剧、动画、科幻、战争、悬疑、动作等多类型影片同台竞技：既有《功夫女足》《年会不能停2！》等大众向喜剧作品，也有《八仙！》《玩具总动员5》等覆盖全年龄段的动画电影；既有《蜘蛛侠：崭新之日》《奥德赛》等工业级视效大片，也有《欢迎来龙餐馆》等兼具艺术性与观赏性的现实题材佳作，不同年龄、不同偏好的观众都能找到心仪影片。

从票房表现来看，国产电影展现出强劲的市场号召力。票房前五榜单中，国产影片强势占据4席。其中，《功夫女足》以22.9亿元票房成绩，在7月中旬强力拉动大盘上扬；国风动画《八仙！》收获豆瓣8.2分高分，拿下15.9亿元票房，充分彰显中国动画创作实力；《欢迎来龙餐馆》上映仅6天票房便突破8亿元，豆瓣评分升至8.5分，淘票票评分创下9.9分历史新高，影片有望冲击30亿元大关，成为“叫好又叫座”的标杆作品。

优质内容供给，有效激活了多元观影需求。灯塔专业版数据分析师陈晋表示，今年暑期档观众结构出现明显变化，成熟观众占比显著提升，40岁及以上成熟观众占比达25.9%，同比提升3.2个百分点，创下历史新高。与此同时，观众性别分布更趋均衡：女性观众占55.6%，持续释放消费带动效能；男性观众占比稳步回升，动作、科幻、犯罪等题材影片成功吸引男性观众回流。在地域维度上，一线城市票房活力显著恢复，深圳、广州票房同比分别增长16.3%、12.5%；下沉市场同样表现亮眼，遵义、贵阳、乌鲁木齐等城市票房同比增速超20%。

“小票根”撬动千亿消费市场

票房数据仅是电影消费活力的一个侧面。今年以来，国家电影局联合商务部开展的“电影+”消费综合试点全面发力，在培育观影消费增量、推动影院消费提质创新、拓宽电影衍生消费赛道、打造“电影+”特色消费品牌等领域多点开花。一张小小的电影票，正串联起“吃、住、行、游、购、娱”多元消费场景。

“电影+文旅”，让银幕风景转化为脚下旅途。公路电影《北回归线以北》上映后，新疆和田地区累计接待游客超833万人次，同比增长近15%，游客消费超52亿元；《功夫女足》让深圳溪涌度假村游客量增长50%以上，大鹏新区旅游收入同比增长16.59%；《给阿嬷的情书》带火广东汕头、潮州等地侨乡古寨与骑楼街巷，更是吸引了马来西亚等海外游客慕名而来。

“电影+商圈”，持续拓展影院承载的城市文化空间边界。在北京，第38届大众电影百花奖举办期间，千万级流量关注度加速转化为城市消费动能，居民持电影票根或投票凭证，可在40余个商圈、1100余家商户享受联动优惠；在杭州，部分影院创新推出“电影+餐饮”模式，观众扫码下单即可边观影边用餐，影院非票房收入占比已经超过票房收入的50%；在西安，不少影院联动儿童艺术院团打造亲子专属剧场，常态化上演儿童剧、开设美育课堂，将观影空间升级为家庭美育新阵地。

国家电影局官网消息显示，2025年中国电影全产业链票房拉动系数约为1∶15.77，即每1元票房收入可带动15.77元的全链条相关产业产值。据此测算，今年我国电影全产业链产值已接近3900亿元。从单一售卖票房到深度开发IP价值、从放映大厅到打造综合消费体验空间，电影产业正依靠强劲的乘数效应，为实体经济注入澎湃动能。

业内人士预判，今年暑期档有望实现票房、观影人次双增长。伴随观众结构持续优化、市场区域布局更趋均衡、影视内容质量多点突破，暑期档不仅为全年电影市场平稳向好筑牢根基，更在光影流转之间，印证着中国消费市场强大的韧性与内生活力。

2026年暑期档电影总票房突破100亿元

2026-08-16 记者 韦夏怡 袁小康 来源：经济参考网

【大 中 小】

截至8月16日记者发稿，2026年暑期档（6月1日-8月31日）档期总票房（含预售）已突破100亿元。《功夫女足》《八仙！》《蜘蛛侠：崭新之日》《欢迎来龙餐馆》《给阿嬷的情书》暂列档期票房前5名。

灯塔专业版数据分析师陈晋分析认为，今年暑期档整体表现稳定，截至8月16日总票房同比增长3.2%，同时观影人次达2.74亿，同比增长5.7%；平均票价36.5元，同比下降2.4%，市场“以价换量”效果明显。业内人士表示，下周暑期档还将迎来“七夕”，由朱一龙主演的《空枪》即将上映，今年暑期档有望强势收官，为全年电影市场平稳向好打下坚实基础。

具体电影方面，陈晋分析称，国产电影表现尤为亮眼，在档期票房前五位中占据四席。《功夫女足》以22.9亿元票房在7月中旬强势带动暑期档票房上扬；国风动画《八仙！》豆瓣评分8.2分，斩获15.9亿元票房，位列第二，充分展现了国产动画的创作实力与市场号召力。《欢迎来龙餐馆》豆瓣评分由8.4分上涨至8.5分，淘票票评分9.9分创平台历史新高，影片上映6天票房已突破8亿元，市场表现亮眼，根据灯塔AI票房预测，影片有望冲击30亿元，成为国产电影“叫好又叫座”的又一经典案例。

题材类型方面，暑期档影片也全面开花，喜剧、动画、科幻、战争、悬疑、动作等多类型影片同台竞技，精准匹配消费者多元需求。“这其中，既有《功夫女足》《年会不能停！2》等面向大众的喜剧作品，也有《八仙！》《玩具总动员5》等覆盖全年龄段的动画电影；既有《蜘蛛侠：崭新之日》《奥德赛》等工业级视效大片，也有《欢迎来龙餐馆》等兼具艺术性与观赏性的现实题材作品，不同年龄、不同偏好的观众都能找到适配内容。”陈晋介绍。

观影人群方面，灯塔专业版数据显示，暑期档成熟观众占比显著提升——40岁及以上观众占比达25.9%，同比提升3.2个百分点，创历史新高；30-34岁群体占比21.5%，同样保持稳步增长。

女性观众依旧是观影市场的核心力量，占比达55.6%，持续发挥消费带动作用。不过，今年暑期，男性观众占比也在稳步回升。“这反映出今年影片类型覆盖面更广，动作、科幻、犯罪等题材有效吸引了男性观众入场，整体受众结构更加均衡。”陈晋表示。

另外，一线城市暑期观影活力显著恢复，票房占比达19.1%，较去年微升0.2个百分点，深圳、广州票房同比分别增长16.3%、12.5%，表现极为突出，西南地区的成都、重庆市场表现同样亮眼，票房同比增长15.0%、12.2%。下沉市场中，遵义、贵阳、乌鲁木齐等城市票房同比增速超20%，展现出强劲增长势头。

在陈晋看来，今年暑期档有望最终实现票房与人次的双增长，观众结构持续优化、市场布局更均衡、内容质量实现了多重突破，为后续电影市场的表现注入了充足信心。

text:
数据读懂2025年中国电影市场，为什么是动画赢麻了_快播影视

摘要：国家电影局数据，2025全年电影票房为518.32亿元，同比增长21.95%，城市院线观影人次为12.38亿，同比增长为22.57%，国产影片票房为412.93亿元，占比为79.67%。全年票房过亿元影片共51部，包括国产影片33部。

国家电影局数据，2025全年电影票房为518.32亿元，同比增长21.95%，城市院线观影人次为12.38亿，同比增长为22.57%，国产影片票房为412.93亿元，占比为79.67%。全年票房过亿元影片共51部，包括国产影片33部。

年度票房前十名的影片分别为《哪吒之魔童闹海》《疯狂动物城2》《唐探1900》《南京照相馆》《731》《浪浪山小妖怪》《捕风追影》《封神第二部：战火西岐》《熊出没·重启未来》《阿凡达3》，前十影片里国产片占据八席，进口片占据两席。

上海依然是国内最大的票仓城市，2025年以25.42亿元继续领跑全国城市票房榜，比2024年21.53亿元上涨18%左右。

根据猫眼专业版数据，全年共有八部电影票房破十亿，年度票房冠军《哪吒之魔童闹海》以超154亿的超高成绩遥遥领先，单片票房占比近三成。此外，年度票房前十名的影片中，有四部是动画电影，在《哪吒之魔童闹海》《疯狂动物城2》等重点影片带动下，2025年动画电影总票房实现飞跃式增长。

2026年1月1日，猫眼研究院发布《2025中国电影市场数据洞察》（以下简称《洞察》）。《洞察》显示，2025年中国电影市场在结构调整中，呈现出积极态势，头部影片带动，强IP影片助推，为市场注入增长动力。与此同时，中国电影市场仍有发展空间。猫眼研究院认为，面对市场和观众喜好的不断变化，需要在类型成熟度、情绪共鸣能力和市场可持续性之间，建立新的平衡。

从整体表现来看，2025年中国电影市场在多重因素影响下实现大幅回暖。

从票房分布来看，2025年电影市场在规模修复的同时，结构也在逐步调整。全年票房TOP10新片中，4部超30亿，8部超10亿。全年国产片票房占比略高于去年，10亿+国产新片数量与去年持平，但1-5亿及5-10亿区间的国产片累计数量同比去年大幅下降，“头部集中度高、腰部塌陷”的问题依旧存在。

从区域结构来看，电影消费的下沉趋势进一步加强。近三年，三四线城市票房占比持续提升，2025年下沉市场贡献度达到近五年来的最高水平。与此同时，新用户和低频用户占比同比上升。随着影片进入下沉市场，电影消费的覆盖面和纵深不断拓展，为行业探索更广阔的发展空间，激活更深层的增量市场。

在2025年的电影市场中，动画电影成为最受关注的亮点之一。数据显示，近三年动画电影上映数量整体保持稳定，在《哪吒之魔童闹海》《疯狂动物城2》等重点影片带动下，2025年动画电影总票房实现飞跃式增长，57部影片贡献了超250亿票房，对全年票房结构产生了显著影响。

从观众结构来看，动画电影的受众基础不断拓宽。一方面，18至30岁的年轻用户在内容平台上保持高度活跃，为影片宣发和口碑传播提供了重要助力；另一方面，30岁及以上观众占比保持稳定，成为动画电影票房的重要支撑力量。《哪吒之魔童闹海》在春节档上映，家庭观影比例明显提升，动画电影在亲子和家庭观众中的吸引力进一步增强。

IP驱动效应在动画电影中表现尤为明显。2025年，动画电影IP占比持续保持高位，首映日预售能力相对突出，部分影片复购率显著高于市场平均水平。《洞察》显示，《哪吒之魔童闹海》二刷比例以绝对领先优势居全年首位；日本动画电影《鬼灭之刃：无限城篇 第一章 猗窝座再袭》凭借成熟的IP基础和稳定的粉丝群体，多刷观影特征明显；《疯狂动物城2》续写狐兔CP，人物关系成为讨论焦点，辐射更大范围的泛娱乐受众。此外，《浪浪山小妖怪》则在题材和表达方式上不断创新，成为成年观众投射现实情绪和社会议题的内容载体，也提升了中国动画市场的想象空间。

除了动画类型的突出贡献以外，2025年电影市场涌现出的不同变化也反映出观众审美和消费习惯的持续演进。国产片不断转变创作思路，从宏大叙事转向平民视角，在旧内容中寻找新切口，并利用视听层面和类型题材的差异化呈现给观众带来丰富的情绪体验。进口片方面，超英片票房量级缩水严重，尤其是2020年以来，超英片的社交和家庭观影属性均明显下滑，单人观影比例上升，中高频观众成为票房主力，IP生命力亟需新故事延续。

猫眼娱乐市场分析师赖力表示，2025年电影市场在结构调整中保持了稳中有进的发展态势，多个重要档期在爆款影片的支持下，表现超出预期，诞生了多项新纪录，给行业和观众们带来了惊喜。同时，市场冷热不均的现象依然严峻，传统意义上的“大片模型”不再是票房的绝对保障，这些变化也给从业者们带来了新的启示。整体上看，中国电影市场受众基础深厚，具备广阔的发展前景和上升空间。如何持续地吸引观众注意力，创作出更加符合观众喜好，兼具热度、口碑和新鲜度的优质内容，将成为未来行业长期面临的重要课题。也期待随着内容供给不断优化、观众需求日趋多元，2026年的电影市场能够不断探索、积极前进，持续释放新的增长潜力。

# 全产业链产值破3800亿！“电影+”撬动文旅全域消费活力

 2026-08-09 22:16:07 来源: 北青网-北京青年报 北京 举报 

据网络平台数据

2026年暑期档电影票房已超85亿元

全年票房已超242亿元

中外影片陆续上映

观影人次和放映场次双创新高

今年暑期档影片类型丰富、题材多元，超120部中外影片陆续上映，已连续一个月单日票房超亿元。

 

其中，国产动画电影《八仙！》票房已突破14亿元，暂列全年动画电影票房榜第一。该片还将登陆全球多个国家和地区。

 

进口影片《蜘蛛侠：崭新之日》目前位列暑期档票房榜第三位。影片于7月29日在中国内地领先全球上映，比北美提前两天，体现了好莱坞对中国市场的高度重视。

 

职场喜剧《年会不能停！2》延续前作轻松搞笑风格，讲述新老打工人相见，整活不能停的爆笑喜剧故事。

 

此外，电影《欢迎来龙餐馆》仅点映及预售票房就取得超8000万元的成绩，该片将于8月11日上映，影片讲述了远赴海外担任中餐馆主厨的徐福，与大堂经理马俊生将“龙餐馆”经营得蒸蒸日上，却突遭战争爆发的一系列故事。

 

随着《欢迎来龙餐馆》还有《奥德赛》等一系列中外影片上映，暑期档电影票房还将迎来一波高峰。

 

除了票房一路走高，还有几组亮眼数据对于稳固中国电影市场基本盘格外重要，截至8月9日中午——

- 今年暑期档放映场次超3022万场，同比增长6.3%；
- 观影人次超2.3亿，同比增长5%；
- 暑期档平均票价36.3元，同比下降3.2%，创近5年来暑期档最低，观影成本持续降低。

此外，据国家电影局统计，截至7月底，今年全国净增影院363家，银幕增加2215块，成为“15分钟便民生活圈”的新供给，让看电影更加进入人们日常生活。

电影全产业链产值突破3800亿元

“电影 +”撬动文旅全域消费活力

随着暑期档电影票房持续走高，丰富的“电影 +”活动拉动消费链不断延伸，今年电影全产业链产值已超过3800亿元。一部影片带火各地好景，一张电影票激活全域消费。

如今，电影院正从单一观影功能，向集社交、消费等于一体的综合性文化体验空间转型。今年以来，在国家电影局联合相关部门推出的“2026电影经济促进年”带动下，电影从“人气流量”持续转化为“消费增量”。一张电影票串联起观影、出游、体验、消费长产业链。据测算，今年电影全产业链产值已超过3800亿元。

 

“跟着电影去旅游”成为消费新潮流，国产动画电影《八仙！》以传统神话故事为灵感，创新演绎独具东方美学的蓬莱仙境，上映以来口碑票房一路走高。随着影片的热映，电影画面里云海青山、亭台楼阁的取景地也成为暑期旅游的热门打卡地，四川成都青城山景区正是其中之一。

 

影片中，八仙盘下的小道观门口，那棵古树的原型，正是青城山天师洞道观前树龄约1900年的天师银杏树。如今银杏树枝头系满了祈福红绳，与电影中“古树寄愿”的场景高度契合。

 

紧跟电影热度，当地推出“仙山过暑假·跟着八仙游青城”等“电影+文旅”活动，通过食宿惠民政策、凭电影票享观剧优惠等措施，激发文旅消费的多元活力。

 

除了秀美的自然风景，电影中古色古香的建筑也成为观众“跟着电影去旅游”的选择。在山西大同，影片的另一取景地悬空寺景区也迎来客流高峰。距今已有1500多年历史的悬空寺始建于北魏时期，是我国现存最早、保存最完好的高空木构摩崖建筑群。故事中，钟离权与吕洞宾阳台对峙、品茶论道的桥段，场景设计就参考了悬空寺的样貌。

光影魅力延伸文化体验

除了撬动文旅消费场景，电影也成了传播优秀传统文化以及地方文化的载体，围绕暑期热映影片，各地以亲子研学游、沉浸式情景演绎等多种形式，将银幕间光影魅力延伸为文化的深度体验。

这个暑期，电影《给阿嬷的情书》以真挚情感引发海内外观众的共鸣，也让侨批文化重新走进大众视野。

 

随着影片热播，福建多个侨乡迎来了暑期旅游高峰，侨批文化研学也成为热门主题，当地推出了丰富的体验活动与文旅线路，让观众能沉浸式感受侨批背后深厚的家国情怀。

 

福建省档案馆馆藏侨批文物数量达五万余件，暑期以来，这里特别设计的“百年跨国两地书——福建侨批”展，成为市民游客的热门打卡点，馆内免费开放285件（组）珍贵档案，让大家一口气看完侨批百年。

 

游客 马煜程：来到福建省档案馆，看见这5万余封侨批文物，以及在电影里面那封没有寄出去的侨批。这就是侨批文化的缩影。

 

游客 陈静涵：我们身为观众，身为后代，也可以从这些侨批当中拼凑起一个属于那个时代的许多奋斗者的身影。

 

此外，各地还推出公益电影惠民放映等活动，丰富家庭观众的文化生活。暑假期间，山东济南的这家影城每逢周末都格外热闹，儿童公益观影活动吸引众多亲子家庭齐聚影厅。

 

今年暑假，当地面向全区少年儿童，精选国产动画及适龄影片，为儿童及家庭观众打造兼具教育性、趣味性与亲子互动的光影体验，点亮孩子们的假期生活。

（总台央视记者 侯军 邵舒宽）

text:
Ten outstanding data projects win the Sigma Awards 2024 competition

# Ten outstanding data projects win the Sigma Awards 2024 competition

/ 10 min read

Illustration partially made using generative AI

### There were 52 entries from 22 countries in the Sigmas 2024 Shortlist. Our Prize Committee went through the list and picked the top 10. We're now delighted to announce the winners of the Sigma Awards 2024 for data journalism.

Together they represent the best of data journalism from 2023. Congratulations to all the people credited in these incredible pieces of data journalism and to all those who've sent their projects in. You've helped us compile the best data-driven projects of the past year, an invaluable contribution that helps us monitor the evolution of our field.

The 10 winning entries were revealed on 22 March 2024, during a livestream on the Sigmas YouTube channel. You can rewatch it and comment via this link.

Sigma Awards 2024 Winners RevealYouTube

## Here is the list of the Sigma Awards 2024 winners:

How China is tearing down Islam Published by The Financial Times Country/Area: United Kingdom Credits: Peter Andringa, Irene de la Torre Arenas, Max Harlow, Sam Joiner, Joe Leahy, Lucy Rodgers, Eva Xiao, Yuan Yang, and Sun Yu.

How China is tearing down IslamThousands of mosques have been altered or destroyed as Beijing’s suppression of Islamic culture spreadsFinancial Times

Comment from the prize committee:

> It's not a secret that the Chinese government detained hundreds of thousands of Turkic Muslims in Xinjiang. The Financial Times was able to find an innovative way to showcase an even broader suppression of Islamic culture in China. The team behind "How China is tearing down Islam" built a database of 4,450 buildings and manually reviewed each one of them for accuracy. Many reporters based in China pursued this story at great personal risk. This investigation is the first to document the scale and the spread of the Chinese government's policy to remove Arabic-style features from the street. This entry successfully combined photos, videos, data visualization and coherence page design to tell a powerful story.

---

Humans are biased. Generative AI is even worsePublished by Bloomberg Country/Area: United States of America Credits: Leonardo Nicoletti, Dina Bass, Chloe Whiteaker, Jillian Ward

Humans Are Biased. Generative AI Is Even WorseText-to-image models amplify stereotypes about race and gender — here’s why that mattersBloomberg

Comment from the prize committee:

> As Generative AI models have made rapid advances in their ability to generate text or imagery, one of the things that we have seen is that biases that are baked into training data can be amplified in the output from models. To produce “Humans Are Biased. Generative AI is Even Worse,” Bloomberg journalists prompted text-to-image models to create more than 5,000 images of workers with various jobs, as well as people associated with crime, and then compared the resulting images with government data on the actual race and gender of those people in those groups. The resulting analysis showed how the models perpetuated stereotypes, even taking them to extremes greater than those in the real world, and used well-executed and creative visuals to clearly demonstrate that to readers.

---

Inside the Suspicion Machine Published by Lighthouse Reports, WIRED, Vers Beton, OpenRotterdamCountry/Area: Netherlands Credits: Gabriel Geiger, Eva Constantaras, Justin-Casimir Braun, Htet Aung, Evaline Schot, Saskia Klassen, Romy van Dijk, Dhruv Mehrota, Morgan Meaker, Matthew Burgess, Kyle Thomas, Alyssa Walker, Raagul Nagendran, Hari Moorthy, Ishita Tiwari, Danielle Carrick, Lily Boyce, Andrew Couts, James Temperton, Daniel Howden, Eeva Liukku, David Davidson, Willemijn Sneep, Sascha Meijer

# Research on the impact of climate change in Uruguay achieves media and social impact

By

- April 11, 2023

Republish

For the first time in Uruguay, a team of scientists and journalists analyzed different databases on the flood line and its impact on the population and relevant infrastructure along the coast of Montevideo. The result was the research piece"The submerged city," winner of the 2023 Sigma Awards that celebrate the best data journalism in the world.

"The Submerged City" is data journalism executed with vision. The Amenaza Roboto [Roboto threat] project is a great example of journalism as a trigger for good, as the team's findings will most likely shape Uruguay's climate-related policies for years to come. It is also a data-driven effort that can inspire others around the world to tackle the same topic in the same clean and visually compelling way," said the Sigma Awards jury during the announcement of the decision in March.

The idea for doing this research came from Miguel Ángel Dobrich, journalist and director of Amenaza Roboto; and Gabriel Farías, data journalist and leader of the Special Projects Desk at Amenaza Roboto. Dobrich, who was part of the second cohort of the Oxford Climate Journalism Network of the Reuters Institute at Oxford University in 2022, took advantage of the opportunity to present "The Submerged City" project at the Open Climate Data Competition of the Uruguayan Ministry of Environment, where he obtained seed funds to make his vision a reality.

"After having intense conversations about best practices with journalists we admire, such as Surya Mattu (formerly at The Markup, Lead of CITP's Digital Witness Lab at Princeton University) and Luis Melgar (graphics reporter at The Washington Post), we put together an interdisciplinary and multicultural team — made up of members from Uruguay, Argentina and Mexico — with whom we worked on 'The Submerged City,'" Dobrich told LatAm Journalism Review (LJR).

With this research, the Roboto Threat team that was founded in 2018 as a platform devoted to technology and science journalism inaugurated its data and climate change journalism unit.

"The Submerged City is a data-driven effort that can inspire others around the world to tackle the same topic in the same clean and visually compelling way”, said the Sigma Awards jury during the announcement of the decision.

"We chose this topic because it seemed relevant to us, and journalism exists to serve the public, our communities...I am convinced that in the ‘Global South,’ small newsrooms have the opportunity to cover topics that big media cannot," Dobrich said.

### Methodology

The final team of "The Submerged City" was formed by Miguel Dobrich and Gabriel Farías together with scientists and technologists from different fields: Natalie Aubet, Uruguayan geoscientist and data scientist; Nahuel Lamas, Argentine specialist in geospatial images; Matilde Campodónico, Uruguayan photographer; and Antar Kuri, Mexican designer.

According to the producers, "The Submerged City" was carried out in four stages: data acquisition, development of an integrated database, creation of thematic maps, and narrative. Among the data used were those of the Uruguayan Ministry of the Environment, the National Institute of Statistics (INE, by its Spanish acronym), the Ministry of Social Development, and the Municipality of Montevideo, among others. Flood areas were extracted from the report National Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change and Coastal Zone Variability in Uruguay (2021).

# ‘Remarkable Diversity’…‘Confronting Some of the Most Urgent Issues of Our Time’: Announcing the 2026 Sigma Awards Shortlist

GIJN Sigmas

 Mar 2, 2026 / 4 min read 

Illustration: Louiza Karageorgiou for GIJN

The Sigma Awards – the premier international data journalism competition – attracted 543 entries from 84 countries for the 2026 iteration. And we at GIJN – in this, our second year of hosting the prize – are delighted to announce the shortlist of this year’s Sigma Awards.

A diverse panel of Sigma jurors chose a total of 31 outstanding data journalism projects and portfolios — 26 of the former, five of the latter — as finalists. This esteemed group hails from 23 different countries and territories around the globe.

Subjects tackled by these shortlisted projects range from Russia’s recruitment of foreign mercenaries and algorithmic failures in Peruvian social programs to the deepfake targeting of female journalists and lead poisoning from car battery supply chains. Several projects offered interactive maps, where – with just a click – readers could identify everything from tax havens to heat islands in their local area. And some of the pressing global topics explored through their innovative data sourcing and visualization include hidden deforestation, ongoing slave labor, sanctions evasion, and the links between domestic investments and unjust foreign wars.

In order to encourage the most innovative data projects, the Sigmas do not feature any topic or format categories. Instead, they are divided only between Single Projects and Portfolios (larger bodies of data journalism work).

Indeed, jurors noted that story formats among the 2026 finalists include podcast investigations, long-form serialized reporting, interactive databases, explainer projects, and visually-driven efforts that combine maps, charts, video, and illustration.

This year, the convenor of the Sigma jury is GIJN Turkish editor Pınar Dağ, who is also co-founder of the Data Literacy Association (DLA), Data Journalism Platform Turkey, and DağMedya, and a data journalism lecturer at Kadir Has University in Istanbul.

"The shortlist demonstrates remarkable diversity not only in geography but also across categories and formats,” Dağ points out. “We see a strong balance between investigations, visualizations, the use of innovation and tools, open data projects, and substantial portfolios from leading data teams.”

Veteran Sigma jurist and competition officer Kuek Ser Kuang Keng also notes that this year’s entries included many more projects from small newsrooms using advanced and innovative data methodologies. "The quality of this year's entries is beyond the expectation of many judges,” he adds.

Dağ says notable methodologies employed by finalist teams included open source intelligence research, cross-border collaboration, satellite imagery analysis, technological experimentation, and audience-centered design.

“Thematically, the shortlisted projects confront some of the most urgent global issues of our time,” she explains. “War and geopolitical conflict are addressed through cross-border investigations into sanctions evasion, shadow warfare, mercenary networks, oil smuggling, and the theft of children’s identities. Human rights and immigration feature prominently, alongside corruption, organized crime, and the misuse of public funds. Environmental investigations are particularly strong this year.” (See the 2025 Sigma winners here.)

北漂青年2026年春节返乡观察：从裁员后的身份焦虑到乡村观念变迁，记录小县城人情世态与代际和解，展现中国基层社会正在发生的微妙变革。 ## 1. 职业观念的重构 - 农村对"不上班"态度趋于宽容，邻里对半年花8万旅游的年轻人表示理解 - 海外就业成新选择，发小在印尼从事镍冶炼工作，月薪过万且包往返机票 - 作者经历两次裁员后，首次以"无标签"状态返乡，观察社会评价体系变化 ## 2. 代际关系的演变 - 父辈仍保持高强度劳动习惯，60岁叔叔回忆年轻时2小时人力装20吨铁 - 女性地位显著提升，邻居回忆40年前除夕包饺子却吃不到的辛酸往事 - 父子达成"不上班"共识：保持身心健康、不触犯法律底线为基本原则 ## 3. 春节习俗的进化 - 走亲访友模式简化，五兄弟家族改为年度聚餐制，取消礼品互赠 - 牛奶礼品销量下降，反映农村人情往来从形式主义向实用主义转变 - 抖音成为新社交货币，方言博主粉丝破千即具社区影响力 ## 4. 城乡共有的生存哲学 - "活给别人看"的心理普遍存在，农村尤甚但城市同样存在 - 春节成为唯一合法休息期，多数商铺全年仅春节歇业 - 家长里短构成重要社交资本，信息交换满足深层心理需求 ## 5. 身份认同的转变 - 失去国企/大厂标签后，作者体验更纯粹的返乡观察者角色 - 家族口述史价值被重新发现，真实故事超越虚构作品 - 离乡心态从"战斗姿态"转为平和接纳，呼应晋商走西口的历史回声

# 从北京到山西，2026春节回乡见闻

崔永旺©

今年腊月二十五回家，正月初六返京。这是我北漂9年里，在家里待的最久的一次。

我非常喜欢我的家乡山西，喜欢山西临汾市襄汾县这个小县城，喜欢我家在农村的院子。

其实回乡见闻我一直在做，每一次回家都会留意。这次特殊之处在于，2025年我在北京经历了两次裁员，这一次回家，没有国企光环，没有大厂光环。以前回家，亲戚朋友都说，或者我也会不经意介绍自己在某某国企、大厂工作，而这一次，在去掉标签后，我想看看会有什么不同。

以下是我从北京到山西，2026年春节回乡见闻。

## 1. 关于不上班

对于不上班这件事，大家越来越“漠不关心”回归常态。过年回家才知道，邻里一个妹妹，不上班半年，旅游了大半个中国，要说把8万块钱花光再回去。她妈妈笑谈。邻里更觉得不是个啥事，直言“姑娘又没花你钱”。放在之前，在农村我挺难以想象的。

## 2. 关于出国工作

发小去年去了印度尼西亚某集团园区工作，从事镍金属冶炼。借此机会，我第一次了解了国外工作、印尼排华事件等。工作管吃管住，月薪过万。空气清新，气温适宜。半年回来一次，往返机票全包。越来越多的年轻人把机会瞄向海外。（我说年后带带我）

## 3. 关于父母

邻居叔叔说，自己年轻时候1个人，2小时，可以装20吨铁到货车上，纯人力。而这样的活儿，当年不止他一人。如今孩子都结婚之后，还是闲不住，还是想干活。（好多乡村叔叔阿姨都是。一方面是赚钱，另一方面似乎是要证明存在感和价值感）

## 4. 关于女性地位

邻居奶奶说起了自己40多年前刚结婚过年的时候，婆婆说，“大年三十儿媳妇就该包饺子”。然后她包了一碗又一碗，别人吃了一碗又一碗。最后却发现没有自己的。这事她印象深刻，她感慨，现在可是不一样啦。

## 5. 关于春节休息

正如“春节是中国人唯一放过自己的日子”。在春节，大大方法地休息、大大方方地串门、大大方方地蹭饭是合理合法的。

春节，赋予了广大乡村地区“合理休息”的权利。很多店铺商家以及老百姓，一年只有春节这一次休息机会。周末、五一、十一这些节假日休息都很少。在这片土地上，有时候让一个人休息很难。我们从贫穷的日子走来，生怕再穷回去。

## 6. 关于在乎别人怎么看我

在广大的农村，很在意“别人怎么看”。单一地说，你不要在乎别人怎么看，很难说服。有时候觉得，生活的一部分是为了“活给别人看”。别人如何看我，这是在做选择，是很重要的一点。奇怪又真实发生着。不过又不止于农村，中国还是一个大农村。

## 7. 关于春节“牛奶卖不动了”

以前大部分农村过年，亲戚串门都是送牛奶。从送山西古城牛奶，到特仑苏、金典等。现在不是关系变了，而是场景变了。

以前七大姑八大姨挨家挨户串门不能空手，现在比如兄弟5个，抽出一天时间一大家族二三十人全部聚会吃饭，说好谁也不给谁带东西。过年只走这一次亲戚。明年、后年轮流。

大家想明白了，送来送去都是给商家赚钱了，而且来来往往也不方便。索性只走这一次亲戚。变化会越来越快，而且随之连带影响也会不小。

## 8. 关于“每个家族都有一部家族史”

我没有加“精彩”二字，这与精彩无关。回了家，你张口问问爷奶、爸妈、亲戚、邻里，关于自己家族、村庄、乡镇、县城的那些故事。你会发现故事多到讲不完。小说、电视剧远远比不上真实生活，尤其是经过时间发酵之后。

## 9. 关于“春节是否回家”

回家的动车上，邻座女生说，姐姐今年还是不回家，“我爸妈求着她都不回来。爸妈说肯定不催婚、不催找对象了，但她还是不回。”后来又说哥哥准备今年买房，看了好多套了，因为觉得现在房子很便宜，以及明年房子会升值。

## 10. 关于“拍抖音”

这次回家，发现拍抖音的人越来越多。许久不见的亲戚打招呼都是，“我见你拍抖音呢。”中国确实大，“抖音”等短视频也很下沉。

也是这次回家才发现，抖音有很多介绍我们附近村庄的博主。好些就是操着方言，一旦粉丝破千，其实影响力是不小的。当然精神正反馈更高。以前觉得这有啥介绍的，其实都有学问。

## 11. 关于春晚

小时候，除夕晚上7点50到8点这十分钟，是最着急的。必须把一家人喊到电视机前一起看春晚，这才是过年。

如今发现，吐槽一句“今年春晚不好看”，已经成了大年初一打招呼方式之一。类似“吃了吧”“转转啊”。

## 12. 关于群发短信越来越少，红包越来越少

这次回家过年发现，除夕的群发微信越来越少了，而相应的，群里的红包也越来越少。从2023年开始吧，一年比一年少。经济状况体现在小细节上。

## 13. 关于那些家长里短和八卦

过年吃饭间隙，听到好多家长里短。恍惚间觉得——过年，就是一场巨大的情报交换。你说东家1234，他言西家5678。

你说没劲吗无趣吗，我可不这么简单地看。甭说别的，回到北上广深办公室，让你最兴奋的不还是八卦吗——“你听说了！咱们公司那谁跟那谁搞一起了”。

我说中国是个巨大的农村，并未对农村有丝毫不敬。我就是农村孩子。意思是咱们大多时候还是“农业思维”。这没有贬义。这似乎就是我们这片土地的特征。

所以说回家长里短。有一瞬间我觉得，大家似乎有时候靠这些家长里短活着，或者说，这些很重要。你言他家家长里短，你又很在乎他家说你的家长里短，大家互相绑定。

## 14. 关于“离家再出发”

过去在国企、在大厂上班的时候，每次离家返京总有一种去战斗的错觉，总有一种“不混个样子不回来”的错觉。我猜，当年乔致庸这些山西后生“走西口”，估计也类似。今年因为不上班，平和很多。

## 15. 关于不上班这件事与父亲达成共识

这次回家前，最担心的就是如何跟父亲沟通不上班这件事。社交平台上，很多人也有类似担心。而父亲与儿子的关系又是微妙且不会表达的。

离开家的早上，我爸开车去高铁站送我，关于“不上班”这件事，这次回家他一个字都没提。我主动说了出来。肯定有观念不一致的地方，但末了，关于基本盘我们惊喜达成一致——不论发生什么事情：

一要保持身体和心理健康，二不要做赌博吸毒大额网贷等违法且一旦犯错绝无弥补机会的事情。

能长期做到这两个基础已经非常好了。在此基础上，等待命运的声音。就足够了。以上一致是对我们大家庭的。

总体来说，今年过年节奏不错。

洗了7、8次碗，做了20个俯卧撑，60个高抬腿。看了50页书。手机使用时间可控。吃了好多顿面，睡了好几个午觉。以及去了心心念念的一些地方，还有村里、邻村的有趣地方。在过去原以为已有够多故事的基础上，又收获了很多关于村子的故事。幸运。

家乡这么多年，村头的大槐树、那些房子都没变，而很多变化又在悄然发生着。农村里的人越来越少，知道那些故事的人也越来越少。我希望可以记录下来，等若干年之后再回看。

新的一年，让我们祝好。

去哪儿2月23日发布的数据显示，假期多出1天，让2026春节整体出游热度创历史新高。外出“旅游式过年”，与返乡“过年式旅游”双双爆火，全国不仅各大知名景区人从众，“家门口旅游”也带火了县城里的景区，一批小城迎来了始料未及的“泼天流量”。更多返乡过年的城里人，也把新的生活方式带进了村里，热门县城春节期间酒店预订量翻倍增长。

60岁以上乘客购买“人生第一张机票”增两成

2026年的超长春节，让“反向过年”从一种小众选择变成了一种潮流。反向团圆，不仅是机票价格“打骨折”的经济账，也是年轻人成为春节主理人后，爱父母的一种方式——过年不再围着饭桌转，而是主打舒服随心。陪爸妈citywalk、喝咖啡，带他们打卡年轻人常去的商圈和主题乐园，让父母过一遍自己的日常生活。

去哪儿旅行数据显示，2026年春节假期，反向飞往北京的旅客中，18%年龄在50岁以上，其中60岁及以上旅客同比2025年春节假期增加超一成。从整体飞行目的地来看，50岁以上旅客最青睐的均为一线城市，北京、成都、上海、广州成为最热门选择。也有不少老人趁着春节团圆解锁了人生第一次飞行，平台数据显示，2026春节假期， 60岁以上乘客在去哪儿平台上购买了“人生第一张机票”的数量增长了两成。

住宿方面，许多年轻人干脆为父母安排高星级酒店，让操劳了一年的老人享受一次酒店服务托底。数据显示，春节期间酒店入住以“阖家团圆”为主要场景，老年人入住量明显提升——2026年春节期间，60岁以上老人酒店入住量同比增长56%，最受老年旅客欢迎的“反向过年”城市包括广州、上海、深圳、北京等。

回乡过年的年轻人选择住进县城酒店

“过年回县城，酒店竟然爆满！”今年春节返乡，一些年轻人选择白天在家和亲人团圆，晚上住进酒店。

去哪儿旅行数据显示，春节期间，旅客入住了全国千余个县城酒店，多地酒店入住量呈爆发式增长。除了大城市、传统旅游景区，回县城过年的年轻人们也“订爆”了县城酒店。

平台数据显示，非旅游景区类县城春节期间酒店入住增幅超60%，多个传统人口大县、劳务输出县城酒店入住量翻倍增长。如安徽阜阳临泉县今年春节酒店预订量同比增1.4倍、湖南常德汉寿县增1.3倍、广西钦州灵山县增1.3倍。从整体入住趋势来看，2月19日大年初三，县城酒店入住人数到达峰值，2月18日至20日期间均保持在高位。

热度蹿升最快的景区是家门口的景区

约满、限流、爆满，成为今年春节各大景区的常态，“前方没有厕所、烤肠和茶叶蛋”冲上热搜。返乡过年的巨大热流也带火了家门口的景区，回都回了，重新发现家乡的美。去哪儿旅行数据显示，2026年春节热度蹿升最快的就是家门口的景区。

从春节期间门票预订来看，河南开封汴河游船景区、湖北武汉东湖梅园、江西景德镇陶溪川文创街区的门票预订量增长最为显著，同比增长都超过5倍。此外，山西临汾哪吒传奇景区、浙江金华诸葛八卦村、江西上饶望仙谷、江西九江庐山的门票预订量，同比均翻番增长。

春节期间，飞往小机场所在城市的旅客量同比大幅攀升。飞往武夷山市的旅客量同比增长1.6倍，增幅领跑全国。一批民俗与非遗特色鲜明、旅游资源独特的小城在春节假期走红。能看太行山水、逛古寨年味的邢台市，以及被称为“宝藏古城”的永州市，机票预订量实现翻番。

外国朋友足迹遍布107个中国城市

9天假期利好出境游，选择出境过年的中国旅客让世界各地有了中国年味。去哪儿旅行数据显示，2月15日至23日，平台上的中国游客飞往了全球近千个城市。最受欢迎的出境游目的地城市多在飞行距离近、签证政策友好、温度适宜的亚洲地区，适合举家出行，泰国重回最受中国游客欢迎的出境游目的地。

今年春节，外国客人也“扎堆”来过中国年。去哪儿数据显示，2026年春节期间使用非中国护照预订国内航班的数量同比增长两成。前十名目的地城市为上海、北京、广州、成都、深圳、厦门、海口、福州、重庆、青岛。

与往年不同，今年外国游客来中国不满足只玩儿一个城市，而是首站选择北京、上海、广州等大城市，然后向内延伸，探索更多中国城市。平台上，外国旅客预订国内航线间机票覆盖了107个城市，外国游客的脚步也延伸到井冈山、万州、阿勒泰、昭通、吕梁、达州、玉林、榆林、通辽、连云港、安庆、二连浩特、汉中、腾冲、惠州、林芝、琼海、鸡西、武夷山、济宁、日照等城市。

摘要：目的地，回家

2014年，央视有一组公益广告，叫《回家》。

广告里的主角，有骑着摩托返乡的贵州农民工，在冰天雪地中摔倒，粘上一身风霜。

有从炎热非洲返乡的东北小伙，在返乡途中，不停加着衣服，一落地，就快乐地扑进冰天雪地。

也有第一次带着女友回家的福建小伙，在风雨中乘着颠簸的小船，终于完成了人生大事。

还有分隔台湾、上海两地得兄弟，时隔60多年，终于能在机场见面，相拥而泣。

十多年过去，国道上不再有浩浩荡荡的摩托大军，反而多了越来越多自驾返乡的私家车。

交通运输部的数据显示，今年春运期间，自驾出行占据主导，预计占跨区域人员流动总量的八成左右。

但不管交通方式如何改变，再颠簸、再难熬，也要回家，就像候鸟归巢。

这是每个中国人，春节的写照。

二月初开始，曾经忙碌的地铁上已然逐渐变得空荡，过年前最为拥挤的，变成了火车站和高铁站。

一趟趟加开的车次，在显示屏不停跳动着数字，检票口提前等待的乘客，脸上也不再是曾经的麻木和疲倦。

哪怕赶车劳累，哪怕人潮拥挤，但每个人的脸上，都写满了期待和幸福。

过去三百多天里，清晨拥挤的地铁、深夜忙碌的加班、老板的刁难、客户的挑剔，以及流水线上重复的劳作、工地上风尘仆仆的工作服，如今都可以抛在脑后。

没有人可以衡量想念这个情绪在过去一年中，被提起了多少次，但春运数据，或许能对过去一年的思念进行总结。

据交通运输部预测，2026年春运期间，中国全社会跨区域人员流动量将达到95亿人次，预计创历史新高。

对于普通人而言，春运从来不只是交通运输上的一个名词，95亿人次，每一个“1”后面都是一个具体的人。

在各地的报道中，我们能看到52岁的外卖骑手背着新衣服和腊肉丸子等年货，终于登上返乡专列。

也有盲人按摩师，在一双双手的传递中，顺利登上返乡的火车。

还有在外地奋斗六年，终于给家里盖了新房子的工人，带着广式腊肠和鸡蛋仔，在镜头前露出幸福的笑容。

也有年纪尚轻的打工人，在异乡被外卖敷衍了整整一年之后，最想念的，还是妈妈做的冬笋炒腊肉。

他们携带不同的故事、奔赴不同的方向、使用不同的交通工具，却在同一个时间节点，做同一件事，那就是，离想见的人，近一点，再近一点。

不论朝向何方，我们都在奔向万家灯火里，属于我们的那一盏。

当“回家”太过艰难，反向过年，也成为了越来越多人的选择。

他们不再返乡，但家，却追随而来。

美团数据显示，2026年春运期间，从三四线城市前往特大城市的车票预订量明显增长。2月初至2月中下旬，“反向过年”的机票预订量同比增长84%。

反向春运的队伍里，那些拎着腊肉香肠的父母在12306的敬老版界面里慢慢学着购票，有人第一次独自坐高铁去城里看孩子，有人第一次坐上长途飞机。

这样的转变意味着，父辈开始放下“你必须要回来”的执念。

在曾经目送孩子远行的背影之后，他们也开始愿意追赶孩子们的脚步，走向那个他们完全陌生的城市。

除了父母和孩子的双向奔赴，如今的过年，也诞生出了更多的选择。

有工人前往新的地方，准备着在新的工地上度过新年。

也有人为了身体不好的父母，准备前往南方过冬。

还有人，选择趁着长假，到想去的地方旅游。

随着交通方式的拓展，中国人的“过年地图”正在前所未有地拓宽。

有人朝旅游景点进发，有人向老家县城前进，有人选择在异乡第一次当家做主，实现团圆的方式变了，但对于团圆的渴望，从来没变。

这样的变化背后，还有一个更隐秘、更深层的变化——

那个曾经必须用“衣锦还乡”来证明自己的时代，正在悄然退场。

过去很长一段时间里，春节返乡对异乡打拼者而言，除了团圆，还是一场带有审视意味的年度汇报。

带回了什么年货？挣了多少钱？谈恋爱了吗？升职了吗？买房了吗？

在饭桌上、在寒暄里、在亲戚看似不经意的试探里，默默丈量着你这一年的成败。

而当越来越多父母能够看到儿女的疲惫和努力，他们不再说，你什么时候回来，而是，我来看看你。

两代人对团圆达成的全新共识就是，你不必功成名就，你只需好好活着。

团圆的质量，不再取决于物理空间的距离，而取决于情感浓度的多少。

与其把七天假期耗在酒桌应酬和无效社交里，不如把完整的、专注的时间，留给真正重要的人和自己。

时至今日，也还有无数人，在路上，在等待，在计算，在盼望。

对于那些在绿皮火车硬座上度过二十个小时的打工人，对于那些因为经济压力无法返乡、也无法接父母来身边的异乡人，春节依然是道沉重的选择题。

但在这个越来越不确定的时代，春节最为重要的，不是面对亲戚，不是年度总结，而是忠于自己，这是对于过去一年的劳累，最好的报答。

那个叫做“家”的地方，不再是一个必须回去的地理坐标，而是一份确定的感情归宿。

家人在哪儿，家就在哪儿。

而幸福，是永远有人敲响那扇门，说一句：

“过年好。”

时代在变，归乡的方式在变，团圆的形式在变，但刻在中国人骨子里的乡愁，从未改变。

那些奔波的脚步，那些滚烫的思念，那些无声的牵挂，都是为了奔赴一场名为“家”的约定。

无论是挤在拥挤的列车上，还是行驶在宽阔的公路上；无论是在熟悉的老家，还是在陌生的城市；无论是衣锦还乡，还是平淡归来，只要身边有牵挂的人，心中有惦念的家，便是最好的春节。

又是一年春运落幕，人口大迁徙的喧嚣渐渐平息，万家灯火中，皆是团圆的模样。

那些曾经的疲惫与奔波，都在亲情的温暖中化为虚无；那些曾经的思念与期盼，都在相聚的时光里得以圆满。

而当春节的烟火散尽，人们又将收拾行囊，再次奔赴远方，带着家人的期盼，带着团圆的力量，开启新一年的打拼。

因为他们知道，无论走多远，无论飞多高，总有一盏灯为他们亮着，总有一群人在等他们回家。

明年，这场关于归乡的约定，依然会如期而至，这是刻在中国人血脉里的执念，也是最动人的人间温情。

title: 返乡潮涌春意浓 乡村振兴正当时——2026年春节返乡创业热潮观察
text:
返乡潮涌春意浓 乡村振兴正当时——2026年春节返乡创业热潮观察

## 返乡潮涌春意浓 乡村振兴正当时——2026年春节返乡创业热潮观察

2026年2月21日

---

春节假期刚刚过半，全国各地已掀起一股返乡创业的热潮。与往年不同，今年的春节返乡季呈现出前所未有的新气象——年轻人不再只是匆匆过客，而是带着资金、技术和梦想回到家乡，成为乡村振兴的生力军。

县城酒店一房难求背后的新趋势

“今年春节，我们县城的酒店提前一个月就被预订一空了。”江西省吉安市泰和县某酒店经理王先生告诉记者，从大年三十到正月初六，酒店客房全部爆满，其中80%的客人都是返乡过年的年轻人。

这一现象并非个例。在全国多个县城，春节期间酒店入住率创下历史新高。据携程数据显示，2026年春节期间，三四线城市及县域酒店预订量同比增长超过150%，其中返乡探亲人群占比达到65%。

“过去年轻人回家过年，都是住在亲戚家或者自家老宅。现在不同了，很多返乡的年轻人选择住酒店，一方面是为了方便，另一方面也是为了考察家乡的营商环境。”中国社会科学院农村发展研究所研究员张明分析说。

返乡创业座谈会遍地开花

春节期间，各地政府抓住返乡人员集中的黄金窗口期，密集召开返乡创业座谈会。2月11日，重庆市巴南区人力社保局召开2026年春节返乡农民工座谈会；2月13日，湖北省麻城市人社局开展返乡创业服务活动；2月15日，河南省宁陵县华堡镇举行在外创业人士新春恳谈会……

“我们镇41个行政村的党支部书记全部到场，与返乡乡贤、企业家代表面对面交流。”宁陵县华堡镇党委书记李建国告诉记者，座谈会上，返乡人士提出了20多个创业项目意向，涉及现代农业、乡村旅游、电商物流等多个领域。

在安徽省合肥市长丰县马郢村，曾经的“空心村”如今已成为创业热土。村党支部书记王大明介绍，今年春节期间，村里接待了30多位返乡考察的年轻人，其中5人已经确定要回乡创业。“我们村现在有电商直播基地、特色民宿、农家乐，去年村民人均收入增长了25%。”

电商直播点燃乡村振兴新引擎

“家人们，这是我们家乡的特产——泰和乌鸡蛋，纯天然散养，营养丰富……”在泰和县的一个电商直播间里，“90后”返乡青年刘小芳正在热情地介绍家乡特产。去年，她放弃在上海的工作回到家乡，通过直播带货，一年销售额突破300万元。

像刘小芳这样的返乡电商创业者正在全国各地涌现。江西省吉安市泰和县农业农村局局长陈志强表示，2025年全县新增电商企业120家，农产品网络零售额达到5.2亿元，带动就业超过5000人。

“电商不仅让农产品卖得出去，更重要的是改变了农民的思想观念。”陈志强说，现在很多农民都学会了用手机直播、拍短视频，有的还成了“网红”。

政策红利持续释放

乡村振兴战略实施以来，国家出台了一系列支持政策。2026年中央一号文件再次强调，要“强化乡村振兴人才支撑，鼓励各类人才返乡入乡创业创新”。

各地也纷纷推出配套措施。重庆市巴南区为返乡创业者提供最高50万元的创业担保贷款；湖北省麻城市设立1000万元返乡创业扶持基金；河南省宁陵县推出“一站式”创业服务，从项目审批到资金扶持全程跟踪。

“政策支持力度很大，让我坚定了回乡创业的信心。”在广东打拼多年的“80后”企业家张伟，今年春节回到家乡四川达州，计划投资500万元建设一个现代农业产业园。“家乡的变化太大了，交通便利了，营商环境改善了，更重要的是看到了发展的希望。”

挑战与机遇并存

尽管返乡创业热潮涌动，但也面临一些挑战。资金不足、人才短缺、基础设施不完善等问题依然存在。

“最大的困难是融资难。”返乡创业青年李强告诉记者，他计划在家乡发展特色养殖，但缺乏启动资金。“银行贷款门槛高，民间融资成本大，希望政府能提供更多扶持。”

专家建议，要进一步优化返乡创业环境。中国社会科学院农村发展研究所研究员张明认为，要建立健全返乡创业服务体系，提供创业培训、融资支持、市场对接等全方位服务；同时要加强基础设施建设，改善农村人居环境，让返乡人才留得住、发展好。

乡村振兴的未来展望

随着乡村振兴战略的深入推进，返乡创业正成为推动农村发展的重要力量。国家统计局数据显示，2025年全国返乡入乡创业人员达到1120万人，带动就业超过3000万人。

“乡村振兴关键在人才。”农业农村部相关负责人表示，下一步将进一步完善政策措施，优化创业环境，吸引更多人才返乡创业，为乡村振兴注入新动能。

春回大地，万象更新。在这个充满希望的春天里，无数返乡创业者正用自己的智慧和汗水，在家乡的热土上播撒希望的种子。他们不仅是乡村振兴的见证者，更是参与者、推动者。相信在不久的将来，广袤的农村大地将焕发出更加蓬勃的生机与活力。

记者手记

在采访中，记者深切感受到返乡创业者们对家乡的深厚感情和创业热情。他们中有放弃高薪工作的白领，有学成归来的大学生，有在外打拼多年的企业家。虽然身份不同、经历各异，但他们都有一个共同的心愿：让家乡变得更美好。

乡村振兴不是一朝一夕之功，需要久久为功、持续发力。相信在政策支持和社会各界的共同努力下，返乡创业的热潮将不断升温，乡村振兴的蓝图将一步步变为现实。让我们期待，在不久的将来，乡村将成为安居乐业的美丽家园，成为创新创业的热土沃野。

# 春节返乡 超六成受访青年欣喜于家乡交通与基础设施的改善

### 84.5%受访青年准备春节花时间重新逛家乡

作者：王品芝 来源：中国青年报客户端2026年02月13日

 

中青报·中青网记者 王品芝

走一走新修的路，尝一尝新开的店，认一认新建的地标……返乡过年，不少人在与亲友相聚时发现，家乡有很多令人欣喜的变化。

近日，中国青年报社社会调查中心联合问卷网（wenjuan.com），对1334名离开家乡在外地工作求学的青年进行的一项调查显示，84.5%的受访青年春节返乡会专门花时间重新逛家乡。老街区的变化（61.8%）、儿时熟悉场所的现状（57.0%）是受访青年探访家乡时主要关注的。66.6%的受访青年表示，家乡最让人欣喜的变化是生活环境更舒适便利了，60.3%的受访青年对家乡交通与基础设施的极大改善感到欣喜。

受访青年中，离乡1年及以内的占20.4%，离乡1年至5年的占33.1%，离乡6年至10年的占27.7%，离乡11年至15年的占8.2%，离乡15年以上的占10.6%。00后占21.0%，90后占50.1%，80后占28.9%。男性占44.3%，女性占55.7%。

重新探索家乡，受访青年主要关注老街区的变化和儿时熟悉场所的现状

河北张家口的80后杨惠在北京工作10多年了。每年春节，杨惠一家四口都会回家过年，“到家后能马上吃上一口家里人自己磨出来做好的莜面，感觉一年奔波下来也没那么累了”。

杨惠说，以前春节时老家能玩的地方不太多，主要是去亲友家串门。但2022年北京冬奥会的举办，让作为承办地之一的张家口发生很大变化。“现在春节回家后，一家人去滑雪成为了一个固定项目。”

老家在广东惠州的张洋大学毕业后一直在深圳工作，对于家乡的变化，张洋的感触特别深，“粤港澳大湾区的建设让我回家更方便了，几乎随时都能回家”。

春节前一周，张洋回到老家惠州庆祝朋友乔迁新居。“朋友的新居在惠阳，面积140多平方米，离深圳非常近。他们两口子在深圳坪山工作，开车过去只需十几分钟，平时到深圳市中心也很方便。”

在外地上大学的畅舒怡今年回山西老家，感受到了很多惊喜：从高铁站回家的高速公路上，两旁安装了“大风车”风力发电机，望过去特别漂亮，以往拥堵的高速路口经过重新规划，变得更加畅通了。

“打铁花、看花灯、游古镇……从大年初一开始就有接连不断的庆新春活动。”畅舒怡表示，随着家乡的古建被更多人关注，自己也想在春节期间重新去看一看，感受家乡文化的魅力。

调查显示，春节返乡，84.5%的受访青年准备花时间重新逛家乡，其中33.1%的受访青年已计划好要去哪些地方。老街区的变化（61.8%）、儿时熟悉场所的现状（57.0%）是受访青年重新探索家乡时主要关注的。其他还有：自然景观的新样貌（54.4%），年轻人的聚集地与生活方式（43.5%），新出现的书店、展馆等文化空间（38.1%），人们的生活节奏（28.3%），非遗等传统文化的创新发展（22.8%）等。

66.6%受访青年表示家乡最让人欣喜的变化是生活环境更舒适便利

“我在北京的很多朋友在冬季都计划来张家口体验承办过国际赛事的专业雪道，家乡已成为很多人的冰雪运动‘打卡地’。”杨惠说，这几年回家发现家乡热闹多了，“冬季滑雪，夏季骑马避暑，孩子们总是玩不够，不想离开”。

调查中，66.6%的受访青年表示，家乡最让人欣喜的变化是生活环境更舒适便利了，60.3%的受访青年对交通与基础设施的极大改善感到欣喜，44.8%的受访青年发现家乡文化氛围更活跃多元了，43.2%的受访青年为各行业加强数字化与产业升级这一变化感到开心，37.6%的受访青年发现家乡出现了很多新的发展机遇，24.1%的受访青年乐见人们的观念更加开放包容了。

老家在江苏泰兴的王鹏感觉，这几年家乡最大的变化是环境更好了。王鹏说，这些年在国家长江经济带高质量发展的带动下，家乡环境变化很大，家门口的河水越来越干净，白条鱼多了起来。“跟家人开车到太湖边上转悠，看着湖里鱼儿们嬉戏追逐，非常惬意美好。”

“每年回乡，爸妈都会带我好好转一转。小时候常爬的山有了盘山公路，河道治理后，两旁安上了路灯，居民活动广场上的小亭子装上了彩灯，晚上特别漂亮。”畅舒怡说，住在农村的姥姥，生活更丰富了，以前老人们主要是坐在一起晒太阳、话家常，现在村里有了活动室，临近春节还组织了写春联、剪福字活动。

畅舒怡表示，家乡的市容市貌也有了很大改变，住在市区的姐姐很为新开发的几个公园点赞。“公园里有很多免费的儿童活动设施，而且设计非常用心，小朋友们很喜欢去，周末带孩子有了好去处。现在市里的医院时常有三甲医院的医生来坐诊，大家能享受到更好的医疗资源。”

张洋说，港珠澳大桥、深中通道等把粤港澳地区紧紧连接在一起。“去年‘五一’，我和朋友走深中通道去佛山泡温泉，1个多小时的路程就到了。去广州也很方便，这几年我们公司和广州一些企业的合作增多了。”

张洋感叹，粤港澳大湾区的发展促进了人才和产业的融合。“对于深圳、广州等大城市来说，市场更大了，对于东莞、佛山、惠州等城市来说，发展机会多了，城市升级了。”

（文中张洋、畅舒怡、王鹏为化名）

Xr - The Peabody Awards

## ABOUT

By 2010, when Always in Season Island launched, the web platform Second Life had more than 1 million monthly visitors who could create avatars and explore open virtual worlds, called islands, in what was arguably the internet’s first attempt at the metaverse. Second Life was a non-gaming environment, mostly intended for leisure and recreation, such as concerts, social meet-ups, and shopping. But the documentary creators of Always in Season Island sought to courageously and controversially experiment with the platform and confront the ongoing legacy of American racial terror, by challenging their viewers with the power of agency. They recreated, in virtual life, for online visitors to explore, the setting of the August 7, 1930, lynching in Marion, Indiana, when 10,000 white men, women, and children came to watch the torture and murder of two African American men, Thomas Shipp and Abram Smith, and the 16-year old who narrowly escaped, James Cameron. (On that day, a person in the lynch mob came forward to declare Cameron innocent, and the rope was removed from his neck.) By drawing on this historical event, the creators of this interactive documentary experience suggest that passive viewing of documentary might be equated with the positionality of bystandership. Avoiding gratuitous violence, the creators offer their visitors tasks to complete, and prompts to consider, that either encourage or stop the lynching from occuring. Ultimately, visitors intimately learn how their own behaviors can help end dehumanization and violence today.

For creating a virtual world on the Second Life platform (a precursor to the metaverse) to push the conventions of documentary and challenge audiences to become agents of change who can make choices to prevent a lynching in 1930s America, Always in Season Island wins a Peabody.

## ALWAYS IN SEASON ISLAND(2010)

## ABOUT

Notes on Blindness: Into Darkness is a beautifully crafted landmark 360 film project that premiered in 2016, answering a fundamental question about the form at a time when the field of moving image media was unconvinced that immersive experiences were valuable. Why VR or 360, when flat film is a more refined and effective medium?

In Notes on Blindness: Into Darkness, the makers at Atlas V unequivocally answered the question “Why immersion?”, while diffusing the unnecessary binary tension the field placed on the relationship between film and immersive mediums. This project was in collaboration with an acclaimed flat feature film documentary. The pieces seamlessly complemented each other and combined to give audiences the breadth, depth, and embodiment of the story.

While the feature film (Notes on Blindness) told the story of an articulate professor documenting his transition from being a sighted to an unsighted person, the immersive piece gave audiences an experience of echolocation. In effect, the tables were turned, where sighted people shifted from sympathy for someone who “lost” a sense, to a realization that they have been so dominated by eye data inputs to their brain they have become “sound blind.”

Finally, the Into Darkness experience uses beautiful dichromatic moving digitized images that whisper dull soft light to give shape to the soundscape in a delay to illustrate what sighted audiences somehow silenced in the processing of their environment. In short, the immersive and digital equivalent to gorgeous cinematography was achieved in this project. The experience answered the “why immersion?” question with innovative design technique, a compelling experience, an emotional journey, and transcendent aesthetics—all elements of an excellent story.

# Hollow

Hollow Interactive, LLC

Even if you’ve never been within 1,000 miles of McDowell County, West Virginia, you’ve driven through it. McDowell is a stand-in for thousands of American counties, once prosperous communities beat down by plant closings,natural disasters, technology shifts, or changing times. Its population, which peaked at 100,000 in the 1950s, is now down to about 22,000, but its remaining residents hang tough, camouflage aging storefronts with bright, cheery murals, open new businesses, keep faith, and savor the surviving pleasures of small-town, slow-lane American life. The website Hollow is an ingeniously constructed, interactive collage of McDowell County, an immersive experience, a digitized diorama. Visitors can meander at their own pace, track the county’s fortunes over time, see residents’ photographs and art, hear their stories, remembrances and hopes, and contribute their own comments and ideas. For combining imaginative story-telling techniques with web-only capabilities that allow visitors to experience life itself in both specific and universal terms, Hollowis honored with a Peabody Award.

Peabody Digital and Interactive Awards 2022 Winners List

Journey Courtesy of thatgamecompany

The Peabody Awards has revealed the winners for its newest category: digital and interactive storytelling.

Included among the 16 legacy honors handed down by the board of jurors are projects in virtual reality, gaming, interactive journalism, social video, interactive documentary, augmented reality and transmedia storytelling.

Narrative games such as thatgamecompany’s Journey feature among the 16 honorees, with the main credit going to the independent studio’s co-founder and game designer Jenova Chen. The immersive and emotional indie adventure — in which players become a robed figure, seemingly lost in an abstract landscape — often appears on lists of the most impactful video games of all time and has been the recipient of numerous accolades since its launch in 2012.

### Related Stories

### Oscars: Germany Picks Cannes Winner 'Everytime' as Best International Feature Selection

### Awards Categories Set for Cannes-Winning 'All of a Sudden' Actresses Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto (Exclusive)

“To recognize the present and future of storytelling in digital spaces, Peabody has taken the unusual step of looking backwards, recognizing landmark pioneering projects that have shaped and defined powerful stories in interactive and immersive media forms,” said Dr. Jeffrey Jones, executive director of Peabody. “We are honored to highlight these legacy projects and their creators, all of which signal the type of meaningful stories we will be recognizing each year going forward.”

Innovator Phil Yu received one of four special recognitions: the Trailblazer Award for his Angry Asian Man blog which amplifies Asian American voices in media and works to combat cultural stereotypes. Meanwhile, Nonny de la Peña — who is known by many as the “Godmother of VR” — received the Field Builder Award for her work at the forefront of emerging media and VR journalism. These awards were presented by The Revenant director Alejandro Gonzalez Inarritu and Hawaii Five-0 actor Daniel Dae Kim, respectively.

Computer program ELIZA, developed in 1964-66 by Joseph Weizenbaum from MIT’s Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, received the Foundational Award for its use as software that was applicable not only in business and scientific settings, but also in building emotional interactions, empathy and connection.

The Institutional Award was given to Forensic Architecture and architect Eyal Weizman, who launched a series of techniques to advance justice and expose large-scale crimes.

“By honoring these legacy projects and creative innovators, we celebrate dynamic stories that push the limit of what we know storytelling to be across all mediums,” said Diana Williams, chairwoman of the new Peabody Interactive Board. “And we also continue to uphold the Peabody’s mission of supporting visionaries who tell stories that illuminate the world around us and can perhaps evoke societal change.”

title: The State of the World’s 7,168 Living Languages — Information is Beautiful Awards
text:
The State of the World’s 7,168 Living Languages — Information is Beautiful Awards

# The State of the World’s 7,168 Living Languages by Stephen Jones

In similar fashion to the natural kingdom, where plant and animal species range from abundant to endangered, the world's 7,168 languages are also classified stronger or weaker using different scales. One important dimension is language status, classified using the 13-point Expanded Graded Intergenerational Disruption Scale ('EGIDS'). Stronger languages are classified as Institutional, broadly signifying official usage within government, trade and education. In the middle are Stable languages, generally featuring languages with widespread social use within communities across all age ranges.

Weaker languages are classified as Endangered, broadly signifying different degrees of vulnerability, represented by two subgroups: In Trouble - languages where the natural ‘Parent teaching Child’ process is weakening; and Dying - languages where native speakers are elderly without fluency existing in younger generations. Extinct features languages that have ceased to exist within the last 200 years or so and, lastly, Unclassified represents the small group of languages without a current EGIDS classification.

There are vast differences in the number of speakers, writers and signers of languages, ranging from those with than a billion worldwide (e.g. English) down to those with a handful of isolated, elderly users of dying indigenous languages. Our infographic explains the EGIDS scale but, more importantly, shows the distribution of languages according to their language status and the number of speakers.

Our analysis reveals fresh insight into the power of major languages and the weakness of indigenous languages. For example, 6.1 billion people speak one of the 490 Institutional languages used in government, trade and edition; whereas speakers of 3,078 Endangered languages account for 88.1 million individuals. Our infographic is designed to educate and inform people about the scale of potential language loss, and advocate for urgent action to protect and preserve endangered indigenous languages. It is a winner of the prestiguous Editor's Choice award from Visual Capitalist.

title: Languages of the World — Information is Beautiful Awards
text:
Languages of the World — Information is Beautiful Awards

# Languages of the World by stefan pullen

My proposed piece for 2023 IIB Awards is an interactive 3D data visualization project titled "Languages of the World".

With this project I want to challenge the norm and showcase that when executed properly, 3D graphics can captivate and engage your audience unlike anything else. By incorporating interactivity and animation, you can create a dynamic experience that can exceed the capabilities of a static graph.

My goal was to captivate the audience's attention by incorporating an initial playful animation, creating a sense of surprise. Following the animation, the audience is provided with the opportunity to interact with the visualization, fostering exploration and discovery. By strategically concealing certain details initially, the audience is encouraged to delve into the visualization independently. Subsequently, specific language details are unveiled through smooth animations, further immersing and delighting the audience.

The choice of language as the topic was driven by its broad general interest, intended to prompt the audience to search for their own language and compare it to others. The deliberate minimalistic approach to the visual elements ensures that users are not overwhelmed, enabling a seamless and enjoyable experience.

3D graphics are controversial because they often result in some form of data distortion, however I believe they excel in creating an engaging experience when accuracy is not the primary objective. By showcasing this project, I want to encourage the discussion about unorthodox approaches in information design.

title: All the World’s Endangered Languages, by Country — Information is Beautiful Awards
text:
All the World’s Endangered Languages, by Country — Information is Beautiful Awards

# All the World’s Endangered Languages, by Country by Stephen Jones

Global language loss on a catastrophic scale is increasing in likelihood, with vulnerable language numbers rising in every continent, every country, and every corner of the world. Indeed, 3,078 of the world’s 7,168 living languages (43%) are now classified as Endangered, 100s of which face the very real threat of extinction within a few decades if no action is taken. Despite these shocking statistics, though, almost no mainstream media coverage is given to what has become an urgent humanitarian crisis.

Whilst every language matters to the individuals speaking, writing and signing them across the planet, 80% of endangered languages (2,484) exist within just 25 countries. Of those, the top 4 countries alone - Indonesia (425), Papua New Guinea (312), Australia (190) and USA (180) - account for well over a thousand endangered languages. If the governments of those Top 25 countries were to take proactive steps to protect the indigenous languages within their areas, 100s or even 1000s of languages could be preserved for future generations, and we could begin to stem language loss.

This infographic presents the current global landscape of endangered languages using a Voronoi diagram, providing insights by continent and country, with associated statistics for the Top 10 and Top 25 countries. It is designed to educate and inform people about the scale of potential language loss, and advocate for urgent action to protect and preserve endangered indigenous languages.

National Geographic Magazine and NYTimes.com (USA) won both Peter Sullivan Award / Best of Show during the 19th Malofiej International Infographics Awards, organized by the Spanish Chapter of the Society of News Design (SNDE).

The international jury, which met in the School of Communication of the University of Navarra from March 20th to 23th, decided to give two awards, one in print and the other in online. National Geographic Magazine won the printed Best of Show with its graphics ‘Gulf of Mexico’, and NYTimes got the same award in online category because of its job ‘How Mariano Rivera Dominates Hitters’.

The Miguel Urabayen Award to the Best Map went to National Geographic Magazine for their job ‘World of Rivers'. This Award was created six years ago in the honour of Miguel Urabayen, Visual Communication professor and movie critic, who was linked from the very beginning to journalist infographics and Malofiej Awards. In fact, Urabayen was the man who discovered in Argentina the cartographer Alejandro Malofiej and saw in him a pioneer of the genre who has definitely revolutionized the printed media during the last decade. In memoriam of deceased Malofiej, the School of Communication of the University of Navarra created the awards as well as the Infographics World Summit, which is held every year in the Social Sciences Building. # New Narratives team at EL PAÍS takes top prize at Malofiej awards for Covid-19 feature

The ‘Best of Show Digital’ has been awarded to a visual narrative special, titled ‘A room, a bar and a classroom: how the coronavirus is spread through the air’

Jun 18, 2021 - 10:48 CEST

One of the graphics from the prize-winning feature.

The New Narratives team at EL PAÍS has won the top prize at the Malofiej Awards, which are viewed as the Pulitzer Prize of infographics. The awards highlight the best journalistic infographic work published during the previous year. The “Best of Show Digital” category has been won by the feature article “ A room, a bar and a classroom: how the coronavirus is spread through the air,” created by journalists Mariano Zafra and Javier Salas.

The article, which was published in October of last year, has become the most-viewed content in EL PAÍS history, with more than 12 million readers its original Spanish version, and more than seven million in English. The feature uses visual narratives in a simple way to explain how health measures can stop the spread of the coronavirus in three different everyday situations.

> Best of Show Digital for El País (Spain) for the project 'A room, a bar and a classroom: how the coronavirus is spread through the air' #malofiej29 https://t.co/XTo4EaOA9C pic.twitter.com/sEcl4kxUEv
> 
> — Malofiej (@malofiej) June 17, 2021

The article drew praise from a number of international experts, and last month it also won the Best Multimedia category at the prestigious Ortega y Gasset Journalism Awards. The jury at the prizes stated that the article had “not just changed lives, it also saved them,” adding: “At a time when the transmission [of the coronavirus] via aerosols was not being recounted efficiently, [the article] was of huge assistance to millions of readers. It is, what’s more, the perfect expression of public-service journalism, which helps to make decisions.”

As well as this prize, EL PAÍS has also won three more Malofiej awards: a gold and a silver for the same feature, as well as a bronze for “ ccu cgg cgg gca The 12 letters that changed the world,” an article explaining how the genome of the new coronavirus makes it so infectious. The authors were Manuel Ansede, Artur Galocha and Mariano Zafra.

The Malojief are awarded at an event organized by the Spanish chapter of the Society for News Design (SND-E) and the Navarre University’s Communication Faculty. [Skip to content](#main-content)

Now in Public Beta

# Italian American Heritage Archive

An AI-powered oral history platform built for Italian American families — turning a single recorded voice into a publishable heritage story.

[Create a Free Account](https://preserver.italianamericans.com/record)[What's New](https://italianamericans.com/community/whats-new)

The Problem

## Voices are disappearing every month

The generation of Italian Americans who remember the old neighborhoods, the Sunday dinners, the voyage across the Atlantic — they're in their 60s to 90s. Every month, irreplaceable stories vanish forever. Most families never get around to recording them. The process feels too complicated, too technical, too easy to put off.

The Solution

## One link. One tap. One story. Forever.

A family organizer picks a culturally specific prompt, copies a link, and texts it to Grandma. She taps the link, sees one question in giant text, taps one green button, and tells her story. Our Heritage Preserver tool handles everything else — transcription, AI narrative generation, photos, maps, and publishing to the Italian American Heritage Archive.

Getting Started

## Quick Start: Try it in 5 Minutes

01

### Open the Admin Panel

[Go to /admin](https://preserver.italianamericans.com/admin)

This is the family organizer's control center. You'll see the full prompt library organized by Italian American cultural category.

02

### Pick a Prompt

Browse & select

Choose any prompt from La Cucina, La Famiglia, Il Quartiere, or the other categories. Each prompt is crafted to draw out a specific memory or story.

03

### Copy the Recording Link

Click "Copy Link"

The admin generates a direct URL to the elder-friendly recording interface pre-loaded with that prompt. In real use, you'd text or email this to a family member.

04

### Record a Story

Open the link — record yourself

The recording page is intentionally simple: one question, one big green button. Tap Record, tell a 30–90 second story, tap Stop, then Submit.

05

### Process with AI

[Go to /admin/recordings](https://preserver.italianamericans.com/admin/recordings)

Your recording appears here. Click "Process" to run the full pipeline: Deepgram transcribes the audio, then Claude generates the magazine narrative, pull quote, themes, locations, and photo queries.

### Abstract

This project is an interactive data visualization narrative of the oral history of my great grandfather, Hovsep Aghek Yeni-Komshian (Hovsep), born April 2, 1895 to an Armenian family in Kilis, Cilicia, Ottoman Empire. Before World War I and the fall of the Ottoman Empire, millions of Armenians lived throughout what is today Eastern Turkey, their nearly 3000-year history in the region making them one of the oldest indigenous groups of the area. However, today the Armenian presence in Anatolia has largely been erased due to the Armenian Genocide (1915-1923), during which nearly the entire local Armenian population was murdered or forcibly deported by Turkish officials, with a death toll of more than one million. Those who did manage to survive became the Armenian Diaspora, escaping to Syria, Lebanon, and beyond. After fleeing Kilis, Hovsep spent the majority of his adult life in Beirut, Lebanon, where he met his wife Helen, raised five children, and practiced medicine for more than four decades until the outbreak of the Lebanese Civil War (1975-1990), which forced him to relocate, once again, to the United States at the age of 84. Between 1973 and 1983, Hovsep, with the support of his daughters, recorded an account of his life resulting in more than 50 pages of transcribed oral history. This project explores Hovsep's life through his learnings, loves and losses. In the first part, data visualization and analysis with the support of Python's NLTK library are used to illustrate the main themes and sentiments of Hovsep's life. In the second part, an abridged version of Hovsep's oral history is presented through a visual narrative, in his own words, accompanied by photos from family albums and recent travels to Lebanon and Eastern Turkey. Overall, this project uses a wide mix of data visualization and narrative techniques to engage the user in Hovsep’s story. It aims to contribute and build-upon existing methods to

Latvia was free from 1918 to about 1941. 40, when the Germans came in. And then the Communist Russians came in. So they had the lists made up ahead of time. And In June of 1941, they collected 20,000, over 20,000 Latvians and took them by cattle cars to Siberia to work in the Gulags in their mines and woods and whatever. My family escaped because my father was not in the army. He had a bad leg, but he hid in the woods. During most of that year, my sister and I were on the farm. My Grandmother’s Lingo — Distil Immersive

An immersive documentary-game

# My Grand­mother’s Lingo

Charting one young Aboriginal woman’s fight to save her culture by learning her native language, Marra.

For

Wins + Honours

“...awesome!

Amnesty International Australia

Background

My Grandmother’s Lingo is an immersive web documentary that combines voice-activated technology, illustration, animation, and music to tell the story of a young Aboriginal woman from the remote North East Arnhem Land community of Ngukurr – Angelina Joshua.

Angelina’s efforts to preserve her language during a time when many Indigenous tongues are in danger of extinction are at the heart of this work. Once gone, they are gone forever, so we wanted the experience to not only convey Angelina’s powerful story but teach users in a fun and engaging way.

Background

Our approach was to bring the user into the story by creating participatory moments to learn some Marra, Angelina’s mother tongue. By combining cutting-edge voice recognition technology with hand-drawn illustrations from renowned Gomeroi and Mandandanji artist Jake Duczynski and original music from Indigenous music producer Kuren (aka Curtis Kennedy), we were able to beautifully highlight this vital story and encourage greater awareness of the plight of endangered languages.

Appealing to young, curious minds and adults alike, the result is an evocative game-like experience that transcends traditional storytelling methods in favour of something more involved, intimate and ultimately more revealing than conventional web experiences.

Our inspiration

We were first introduced to Angelina through our journalist colleague, Gina McKeon, who told us about a friend she’d made in the Northern Territory. Over many years, whilst reporting for the ABC, Gina would drop in and visit Angelina, to get an update and see how her journey was going. She would sometimes record their interviews, and after a while, she edited together a short audio vignette of Angelina’s story. Hearing her passionately reflect on her mission to save her ancestor’s language proved to be our inspiration. Motivated by a sense of urgency, we assembled a team of talented creatives and technologists to bring Angelina’s story to life.

“The language it’s our identity—culture, totems, countries, and skin names. It’s dying, you know—it’s fading away really slowly.

Angelina Joshua

Education and Learning

## Interactive documentary as a learning resource

Being part game, part animation, My Grandmother’s Lingo considers how gaming technology and voice-activated interactions can engage and teach young audiences across Australia and around the world about underrepresented Indigenous stories. It is being taught in Australian schools to secondary students as part of the curriculum, focusing on F-10 learning areas such as Intercultural Capability, Media Arts, Critical & Creative Thinking and English.

text:
My Family Story — IRENE VAILIKIT

## My Family Story

A storybook creation platform that allows families to share their unique family history with their little ones.

Check out the microsite I created in Webflow and play around with my coded prototype.

## CONTEXT

My Family Story was my capstone project for the MFA in Interactive Media degree at the University of Miami. I worked on this project from October 2021 to May 2022. The capstone requirements consisted of designing a concept that would be considered ready to ship and shows the breadth of skills learned in the program. I conducted research, designed and iterated on the concept, and coded a prototype. This project won “Best in Show” out of 40+ projects during the University of Miami Interactive Media Showcase in May 2022.

## INSPIRATION AND BRIEF

In the last few years, Asian Americans and Asian cultures have garnered increasing attention in the media. From a slow but steady increase in Hollywood representation (Crazy Rich Asians, Parasite, Shang-Chi) to elderly Asian Americans bearing xenophobic attacks during the pandemic eventually resulting in Congress passing the COVID-19 Hate Crimes Act, making it easier for victims and families to report hate crimes. As an Asian American who grew up and lives in a major city where there is a low percentage of Asian Americans, I was interested in building on Hollywood’s momentum of telling an Asian American story, specifically representing the stories of Filipino Americans in Miami.

## HOW MIGHT WE

The questions I sought to explore were based on my upbringing in a tight-knight Filipino community, despite the lack of an Asian American population in Miami.

How might we understand how a Filipino community is created in Miami where there is not a high population of Asian Americans?

How might we understand what are the tenets of a Filipino home (physical, emotional, structural)?

How might we understand the immigration trajectories of Filipino moms/Titas and how that impacts how they form community/home?

## BEGINNING RESEARCH

I wanted to begin my research by interviewing two of my Filipina “Aunties” or Titas -- women who are not biologically related to me, but played a huge role in my upbringing. As a child, I played with their daughters, they picked me up from school and our families have spent every major holiday together. In order to start to tell a broader Filipino-In-Miami story, I wanted to start by understanding their backgrounds and their immigration stories.

My “Aunties” or Titas, with my mom in the middle.

Here is a sample of the questions I asked:

Can you tell me about where you were born and about your parents and siblings?

What was your favorite food that you ate at home?

How did you make the decision to become a nurse and come to the United States?

Do you remember your first day in the U.S.? What was that like?

Who was your community when you first arrived?

How did you choose North Bay Village as a place to live? When did you move to North Bay Village? Why did you choose this neighborhood?

Describe the Filipino community that you are a part of here.

How do you think the Filipino community has impacted your children?

I interviewed both of them on Oct. 23, 2021 for over two hours each and was impacted in a way that surprised me. Both of my Titas were really into the storytelling. Like, really into it. And I learned about their families -- I was particularly surprised to know that both of them came from prominent families in their communities. One Tita’s parents owned a farm that raised watermelon, fish, and pigs. The other came from a family whose father was the city’s civil engineer and her mother was a home economics teacher, despite my Tita never having seen her mother cook for their large family. I realized that I could have known this information at any point, if I had just asked in the 25 years of me having known both of them, but I never took the opportunity to do so.

title: What journalists need to know about accent bias
text:
What journalists need to know about accent bias

# What journalists need to know about accent bias

Linguist Valerie Fridland debunks perceptions around accents that still shape what counts as “proper” speech and what influences hiring, reporting, and audience trust

 

 Jacob Granger 

 February 18, 2026 – 6 min read 

Valerie Fridland, professor of linguistics, University of Nevada. Copyright: Martin Szillat / One Digital Media

When the BBC was established in the 1920s, it set the tone - quite literally - for what "proper" English was supposed to sound like. Received Pronunciation (RP) became the accent of choice for its presenters, a marker of education and authority that dominated British broadcasting for most of the twentieth century. Known variously as the "Oxford accent", "BBC accent", "King’s/Queen’s accent", or "public-school accent", RP was held up as the gold standard for professional speech.

Even in its heyday, RP contained a great deal of personal variation and, like any accent, has been subject to change. Despite this natural evolution, it’s not so easy to shift the idea of a single, “correct” way to speak in the minds of the general public.

Even today, as JournoResources highlights, regional and working-class voices remain underrepresented in UK broadcasting, and accent bias continues to shape who gets heard and who gets ahead. This persistent preference for "standard" speech not only limits career progression for talented journalists but also narrows the perspectives and trustworthiness of news coverage for audiences across the country.

So why do these biases persist? And what can be done to challenge the norm? Valerie Fridland, a professor of linguistics at the University of Reno, sheds some light in her upcoming book, Why We Talk Funny, coming out on 21 April 2026.

The bottom line: there is no single 'right' accent. Accents are not, and have never been, a result of ignorance, indifference or inability. And a journey through history supports this conclusion.

> "Accents are universal, we have them whether we hear them or not," Fridland explains. "And they’ve evolved for all sorts of good reasons."

### Accent bias in newsrooms: The roots and realities

The problem: Stereotypes about "proper" or "correct" speech still shape who gets hired, who gets promoted, and whose stories are told. Biases are not just social snobbery; they're rooted in centuries-old ideas about class, status, and even evolutionary psychology.

Historical context: Fridland traces the origins of RP to the industrial revolution, when class mobility made accent a new gatekeeping tool. Manuals and elocution guides proliferated, teaching the rising middle class how to "sound right" to blend in with the elite. This legacy persists: even today, a regional or working-class accent can be a barrier to entry in elite professions, including journalism.

Evolutionary roots: She explains that humans are wired to notice accents as a way of identifying in-group and out-group members - a survival mechanism that once helped us distinguish friend from foe. This instinct persists, making us unconsciously gravitate toward people who sound like us and, conversely, judge those who sound different.

Modern consequences: In newsrooms, this means that accent bias can operate both overtly (mockery, exclusion) and subtly (unconscious preference for "neutral" voices). Fridland's own experience - her graduate student being singled out for a US southern accent - mirrors countless stories from UK journalists who feel pressure to "soften" their voices or are overlooked for on-air roles.

Cognitive science: Accent bias isn't just about prejudice; it's about cognitive fluency. When we hear an accent we don’t expect, our brains have to work harder, which can make us feel uncomfortable or even less able to understand the speaker. Simply making people aware of this effect ahead of time can help reduce bias in hiring and evaluation.

### So what?

Awareness and training: New

title: 'I didn't speak the Queen's English': Why people worry about their accents - BBC News
text:
'I didn't speak the Queen's English': Why people worry about their accents - BBC News

Mia Tanswell

Mia Tanswell says she became conscious of her accent when she started university

Marc Ashdown

Business correspondent

24 August 2026

Growing up in Manchester, Mia Tanswell didn't give her accent much thought - until her first week at university in Loughborough.

"I knew people were going to notice that I was northern and that I didn't speak the 'Queen's English'," the 22-year-old says.

"Definitely in seminars I would sometimes feel like my accent would sound a bit less intellectual than other people, especially if I was the only northern student in the classroom."

She's not alone. Fresh polling seen by the BBC suggests many workers still see so-called "accent bias" as a problem.

The survey found one in 10 people in Britain feel anxious or self-conscious about their accent in high stakes professional settings such as speaking up in a business meeting.

The research, conducted by the organisation More in Common of more than 3,300 adults across England, Scotland and Wales, found accent-related anxiety in work settings like these was highest among Geordies - from the region around Newcastle - and those with an east London - or Cockney - accent (at 19%), followed by people with a Welsh accent (at 18%).

Around 5% of respondents believed their accent had cost them a promotion, pay rise or senior role. "Brummies" - people from Birmingham - were the most likely to feel this, at 13%.

Respondents with a West Country accent reported the highest rate of having their accent mocked or criticised by colleagues, at 15%, followed by 13% of those with a Geordie accent.

The poll was commissioned by Common Ground, an organisation which aims to promote social cohesion. Its founder, Lara Newman, has worked in construction, property and the built environment industry for more than 30 years, and says she changed her own accent to get ahead in the workplace.

"I am incredibly realistic about what would have happened had I gone to university or gone into the workplace with a strong west country accent," she says. "I felt like that was going to be an issue for me."

Common Ground aims to support people from disadvantaged backgrounds into work but she says one of the layers creating a barrier to them is accent.

"I think there is a problem in the sense that [an accent] implies a level of education or otherwise. It implies class," she says.

## 'I wish it was more Welsh'

Martha Powell

Martha Powell is proud of her Welsh accent

Martha Powell, 24, from Newport in south Wales is proud of her accent.

"I love my accent, if anything I wish it was more Welsh," she says.

But she still fears people "make assumptions" based on her accent so at networking events she gravitates towards others with a Welsh accent.

"I wish I would be able to stand out a little bit more, but I think I adapt my accent depending on where I am in the country."

Softening an accent is common, the survey results suggest, with 13% of Britons polled admitting to changing the way they speak to sound more professional, with Cockneys and Scots more likely to do this.

Benjaimin Aidomoan says his accent has made job-hunting more difficult

A foreign, rather than a regional accent, can also be a barrier. When Benjaimin Aidomoan came to the UK four years ago from the Czech Republic aged 16, he didn't speak a word of English.

He picked up the language, but four years on says his accent has made job-hunting more difficult.

"You can just see on many people's faces, that the expression and the way they are looking at you and the way they are talking to you kind of changes," he says.

Benjaimin, who now works in a restaurant, believes most employers do look beyond accents.

"It's about who you are, how you present yourself, what is your attitude and how hard you're willing to work," he says.

# Is Accent Bias the Last Acceptable Form of Prejudice?

## Judging people based on how they speak is wrong—but also very common.

Posted June 5, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

The way we speak greatly affects how others perceive us -- for good or ill.

Source: Grok / xAI

Most of us are taught, from a young age, not to make assumptions about others based on their appearance.

Or we learn, through experience, that the visible characteristics of a person—their age, ethnicity, body size and shape, or gender identity—are poor predictors of their intellect, status, level of education, or sophistication.

In short, we figure out that judging a book by its cover is problematic at best, and prejudiced and discriminatory at worst.

And yet, many people seem perfectly comfortable with making attributions based on people’s speech, and specifically their regional or nonnative accents. Someone who would never mock a person based on their weight, for example, might feel no compunction about imitating a Southerner’s drawl, or the vocal fry (creaky voice) associated with the speech of younger women.

## A linguist's take

The study of speech patterns like these, and the attributions they engender, is the province of researchers who call themselves sociophoneticists. This rather formidable term denotes linguists who study the social aspects of speech sounds. And the body of research they have amassed provides a fascinating—and at times, rather depressing—account of how language can function as a social cue, and one that can serve to unite or to divide us.

Source: Viking Press / Penguin Random House

I’ve been thinking about accent bias and speech discrimination quite a bit recently, after reading the new book by Valerie Fridland, a sociolinguist at the University of Nevada, Reno (and a contributor to Psychology Today). Titled Why We Talk Funny: The Real Story Behind Our Accents (Viking), she provides an engrossing review of sociophonetic research.

[Full disclosure: I collaborated with Fridland a couple of decades ago, and we are coauthors on two empirical papers based on that research.]

I reviewed Fridland’s previous book about language usage for a general audience—Like, Literally, Dude: Arguing for the Good in Bad English—and greatly enjoyed it (you can find my thoughts here).

I’m happy to report that her latest offering is just as smart and as engaging as her previous volume: it’s an informative, often funny, and always fascinating review of accents, dialects, and language change.

Writing about empirical research for the general public can be a tricky affair. On the one hand, the author wants to present these studies in an appealing way, but on the other, there is a desire to do full justice to studies that frequently have complex designs and not entirely clearcut results. It’s definitely a balancing act, but Fridland navigates between these competing agendas with aplomb.

Readers will learn, for example, about studies showing that people can identify a person’s accent as “like us” or “not like us” in just a fraction of a second. Or that people have strong opinions about what a “beautiful” language sounds like. And potentially controversial topics, like accent and race, are handled with sensitivity.

## Real-world examples

For nearly four decades, I’ve lived and worked in a region of the U.S. called the Mid-South, although I originally hail from the Midwest. Centered on Memphis, Tennessee, the Mid-South has a complex mélange of dialects, and many of these are considered, by speakers of other regions, to be relatively low in prestige.

I vividly remember when a new parking garage was built on my campus, and a recorded voice was employed to alert motorists to “Push button for ticket.” The voice on the recording, however, belon

# Accentism on Trial: Categorization/Stereotyping and Implicit Biases Predict Harsher Sentences for Foreign-Accented Defendants
[CarlosRomero-Rivas](#con1)[https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8413-189X](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8413-189X)[carlos.romeror@uam.es](mailto:carlos.romeror@uam.es),[CharlotteMorgan](#con2), and[ThomasCollier](#con3)[View all authors and affiliations](#tab-contributors)

## Abstract
In this study, participants were presented with two tasks: the Implicit Association Test (IAT), and a mock trial task. In both tasks, the auditory stimuli were produced by native or foreign-accented speakers, and presented either free of noise or mixed with background white noise, to estimate the role of processing fluency on jurors’ appraisals. In the IAT, participants showed positive implicit biases toward native speech, and negative implicit biases toward foreign-accented speech. In the mock trial task, participants gave much harsher sentences to the foreign-accented than native defendant, but only when defendants’ statements were free of noise. Moreover, we found that participants’ implicit biases were a relevant predictor of the sentences they gave to the defendants. Our results suggest that categorization/stereotyping is the main mechanism responsible for the effect of defendants’ accents on jurors’ appraisals, and that members of an estimated group who violate social norms are punished more severely.

title: The endangered Tanka language in Hong Kong: phonological variations and lexical convergence with Cantonese | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications
text:
The endangered Tanka language in Hong Kong: phonological variations and lexical convergence with Cantonese | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

### Subjects

## Abstract

The Tanka people, colloquially known as the “boat people”, are primarily located in Southeast China. Over time, their transition from a maritime to a land-based lifestyle has significantly influenced the languages they speak, particularly through contact with dominant languages such as Cantonese and Hakka. Despite this, the Tanka language in Hong Kong remains under-researched and is now endangered, with its use rapidly declining. To fill this research gap, this study examined the linguistic interactions between the Tanka language and Cantonese in Hong Kong, focusing on phonological and lexical aspects. The study yielded several key findings. First, a comparative analysis of the phonological systems of the Tanka language and Cantonese revealed striking differences in their rhyme patterns and tone evolution from Middle Chinese. These findings underscore significant phonological distinctions between the two languages. However, despite these differences, Tanka and Cantonese speakers can generally comprehend each other due to a shared linguistic structure. Second, a lexical comparison of the Tanka language, Cantonese, and Mandarin demonstrated a considerable connection between the Tanka language and Cantonese, especially among the younger speakers. This generational influence highlights the impact of Cantonese on the Tanka language. In contrast, the Tanka vocabulary diverged significantly from Mandarin, reflecting a unique linguistic development influenced by its historical and social context, while showing greater convergence with Cantonese due to prolonged contact and shared regional influences. Understanding the interplay between the Tanka language and Cantonese provides valuable insights into the origins of the Tanka people. It also contributes to a broader understanding of the typological characteristics of Sinitic languages in Southeast China.

## Introduction

The Tanka people or boat people (水上人) predominantly reside in Southeast China. Officially classified as part of the Southern Han, their traditional settlements span Guangdong, Guangxi, Fujian, Hainan, the coastal regions along the Pearl River Delta, and the Special Administrative Regions of Hong Kong and Macau (Anderson, 1970; Chan, 2012; Huang and Xu, 2018; Yang, 2019; Yao, 2022; Zhuang, 2009). A small population of Tanka people can also be found in Vietnam, where they are recognized as Đàn, a subgroup of the Ngai people (Kani, 1967). As bearers of a unique maritime heritage, their language functions not merely as a communication tool but as a vital repository of ancestral knowledge, rituals, and social cohesion. While many Tanka people have transitioned to a land-based lifestyle, the older generations continue to preserve their maritime traditions. This shift has, at times, led to their marginalization, with the community being labeled as “water gypsies ” (Chen et al., 2022; He and Faure, 2016; He et al., 2022).

The Tanka people are believed to be among the earliest inhabitants of South China, though their origins remain a subject of ongoing research and debate (Cheung, 1991; Fung, 2013; He et al., 2022; Kani, 1967; Luo, 1929; Luo et al., 2020; McCoy, 1965). While previous studies have primarily focused on the cultural practices of the Tanka, their language, paticular in the Hong Kong context, has been largely overlooked. title: Analyzing Maintenance of Heritage Languages in Migration Context: Insights from Cantonese Heritage Language Users in the Netherlands

Analyzing Maintenance of Heritage Languages in Migration Context: Insights from Cantonese Heritage Language Users in the Netherlands

Aholi So Leiden University

1

Abstract 
Despite the global decline of Sinitic varieties other than Mandarin, there is an absence of research 
on the heritage language maintenance on the user’s level. This study proposes the Heritage 
Language Attitude model to explore the dynamics of heritage language maintenance by analysing 
the experiences of 1.5- and second-generation Dutch Cantonese descendants. Through 
constructivist grounded theory, four dimensions emerged: Necessity, Perception of the World, 
Cultural Heritage, and Pragmatic Reasoning. These dimensions reveal how individual experiences 
intersect with broader cultural and societal factors, influencing language attitudes and 
intergenerational transmission outlook. The findings contribute towards a more inclusive and 
effective heritage preservation and heritage language policies. The study calls for community 
driven research to address the needs of heritage communicative communities, urge rethinking 
heritage language maintenance in migration contexts, and offers an analytical framework to 
accomplish this. 
Key words 
Chinese Diaspora, Cantonese, Cultural Heritage, Heritage Language Maintenance, Language 
Policy and Planning 

1 Aholi So is a lecturer at Leiden University’s departments of Chinese Studies and International Studies, specializing in heritage in Asian and European contexts. He is a second-generation Cantonese from the Netherlands. His research interests include cultural heritage and heritage languages of diasporic communities, language policy and planning, and heritage transmission.

1. Introduction 
“[The stories of Chinese people] are not preserved because it is not the norm. 
So, what you often have is stories that are relevant to the majority of society, the 
odds are greater that those are preserved. And that of the Chinese, 
Hongkongnese, Taiwanese, or whatever, in the Netherlands is a lot less. The 
odds are bigger that something will get lost.” (Participant 7) 
The Netherlands is home to various Asian communities, but their voices are not always heard and 
their heritage is not necessarily valued with equity within the broader national discourse. 
According to the above Dutch person of Chinese descent (DCD) I interviewed, East Asian heritage 
in the Netherlands is regarded as far more vulnerable than heritage directly related to the 
Netherlands due to its perceived relevance (or lack thereof) to Dutch society. Indeed, heritage that 
aligns with the majority culture is more likely to be preserved, while that from minority 
communities is often overlooked and at greater risk of being lost (Smith, 2006). 
Cultural heritage is recognized and safeguarded when it has significantly influenced the 
majority culture or is deemed valuable by society at large. For instance, Chinese-Indonesian 
restaurants are inscribed on the Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage in the Netherlands, given

As Thai hit movie How To Make Millions Before Grandma Dies illustrates, the waning use of “dialects” can make it hard for grandchildren to communicate with their grandparents, says linguistics expert Associate Professor Tan Ying Ying from NTU.
